title: India's Tech Leaders Are Demanding a $6 Billion AI Fund. The Anthropic Shutdown Made It Personal.
excerpt: Mohandas Pai wants ₹50,000 crore a year for sovereign AI. Sridhar Vembu says go open-source. Both agree on one thing: India cannot build its future on infrastructure it does not control.
body:
Three days. That is how long Anthropic's newest AI models were available before the U.S. Commerce Department ordered them shut off for every foreign national on the planet.

The suspension of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 12 was aimed at addressing what Washington called national security concerns and cybersecurity vulnerabilities. But for India — Anthropic's second-largest market, a country where TCS had just begun training 50,000 employees on the company's models — the episode landed as something more fundamental: proof that access to the world's most powerful AI can be revoked with a single directive, regardless of contracts, partnerships, or commercial commitments.

Now India's most prominent technology voices are demanding a response that matches the scale of the threat.

Mohandas Pai, the former Infosys CFO turned investor, has called for a ₹50,000 crore ($6 billion) annual fund for AI and deep tech — roughly five times what New Delhi committed under the IndiaAI Mission approved in 2024. Alongside it, he wants a ₹2 trillion ($21 billion) credit guarantee programme to support cloud infrastructure, hardware, and semiconductor development.

"We are way behind and need a national mission to get going quickly," Pai wrote on X, arguing that India cannot afford to treat AI sovereignty as a distant aspiration while its IT industry — the backbone of its services economy — depends on models built, hosted, and governed in America.

""Technology is the ultimate weapon," Vembu wrote."

Sridhar Vembu, the founder of Zoho and one of India's most outspoken tech entrepreneurs, took a different tack. Rather than matching American spending dollar for dollar, he urged Indian organisations to embrace smaller and open-source models, including Chinese alternatives.

"Technology is the ultimate weapon," Vembu wrote. "What can our government do right now? Ensure that orgs in India embrace smaller models, both Indian and Chinese open source ones."

Their diagnoses differ, but their conclusion is the same: India cannot build its AI future on infrastructure it does not control.

The timing is particularly painful. Anthropic had opened its Bengaluru office in February. Infosys had struck a collaboration deal. TCS announced a partnership to equip 50,000 associates with Claude just days before the suspension. Indian startups with cross-border engineering teams — employees split between Bengaluru and San Francisco — found themselves in the absurd position of having half their workforce locked out of the tools the other half was using.

"If your AI team is not made up entirely of U.S. citizens, you are at a competitive disadvantage," said Vijay Rayapati, CEO of Atomicwork, whose product engineering team is based in India.

Not everyone agrees that the primary problem is money. Hemant Mohapatra, a partner at Lightspeed, argued that India's real constraints are talent, compute access, and execution — not the size of government cheques. Training a frontier model costs hundreds of millions to several billions of dollars, he noted, but successful AI companies have historically raised that capital incrementally as adoption grew.

The broader pattern, though, is hard to dismiss. U.S. export restrictions that once targeted only hardware — advanced Nvidia chips, ASML lithography tools — have now expanded into AI software and models themselves. That is a qualitative shift. A country can stockpile chips; it cannot stockpile a model that updates quarterly.

"Even if this is corrected or reversed, the Anthropic episode shows there's no such thing as a geopolitically neutral foreign LLM," said Prasanto Roy, a New Delhi-based technology policy expert. "American AI models are bound to American geopolitics."

For the Indian diaspora working in Silicon Valley, the implications cut both ways. Many hold H-1B visas or are foreign nationals at U.S. AI companies — exactly the people now classified as security risks by broad-stroke export controls. And for the Indian IT services industry that employs millions, the question is existential: if the tools of the trade can be switched off overnight, what is the trade worth?

India's government has not yet responded to Pai's proposal. But the next budget cycle will tell us whether Delhi treats this as a passing diplomatic squall or the wake-up call that Pai, Vembu, and a growing chorus of founders believe it to be.
